content: The ATF1 protein, also known as the cyclic AMP-dependent transcription factor ATF-1, is a protein encoded by the ATF1 gene in humans. This gene produces an activating transcription factor that is a member of both the ATF subfamily and the bZIP (basic-region leucine zipper) family of transcription factors. The ATF1 protein plays a critical role in regulating cellular physiological processes by modulating the expression of downstream target genes involved in growth, survival, and other cellular activities. The ATF1 protein undergoes phosphorylation at serine 63 within its kinase-inducible domain. This phosphorylation is mediated by several serine/threonine kinases, including cAMP-dependent protein kinase A, calmodulin-dependent protein kinase I/II, mitogenand stress-activated protein kinase, and cyclin-dependent kinase 3 (cdk-3). Phosphorylation of ATF1 enhances its transactivation and transcriptional activities, which in turn promotes cellular transformation. Clinical Significance Chromosomal translocations involving the ATF1 gene and either the FUS gene on chromosome 16 or the EWSR1 gene on chromosome 22 result in the formation of chimeric proteins. These fusion proteins are implicated in the pathogenesis of angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma and clear cell sarcoma. Additionally, the ATF1 gene has a pseudogene located on chromosome 6.
